Mindfulness

Wise mind

The place where emotion mind and reasonable mind overlap.

  • Breathe in “wise,” breathe out “mind.”
  • Ask: what does my wise mind know here?
  • Wait for a calm, settled answer.

Mindfulness

Observe

Notice what is happening, without words.

  • Notice sensations, sounds, thoughts and urges.
  • Let them come and go, like clouds passing.
  • Don't push anything away or hold on.

Mindfulness

Describe

Put words to what you observed.

  • Name facts, not interpretations.
  • “I notice my jaw is tight.”
  • A thought is a thought, not a fact.

Mindfulness

Participate

Throw yourself fully into what you're doing.

  • Let go of self-consciousness.
  • Become one with the activity.
  • Do just this, completely.

Mindfulness

Nonjudgmentally

See the facts, not “good” or “bad.”

  • Swap judgments for what actually happened.
  • Notice a judgment and let it go.
  • Don't judge yourself for judging.

Mindfulness

One-mindfully

Do one thing at a time.

  • When eating, eat. When walking, walk.
  • Notice when your mind wanders.
  • Gently bring it back, again and again.

Mindfulness

Effectively

Do what works.

  • Focus on your goal, not on being right.
  • Act as skillfully as you can.
  • Let go of “shoulds” and resentment.

Interpersonal effectiveness

DEAR MAN

Asking for what you want, or saying no.

  • Describe · Express · Assert · Reinforce
  • (stay) Mindful · Appear confident
  • Negotiate

Interpersonal effectiveness

GIVE

Keeping the relationship while you ask.

  • (be) Gentle: no attacks or threats
  • (act) Interested: listen
  • Validate · (use an) Easy manner

Interpersonal effectiveness

FAST

Keeping your self-respect.

  • (be) Fair to yourself and to them
  • (no excess) Apologies
  • Stick to your values · (be) Truthful

Interpersonal effectiveness

Validating others

Show that their feelings make sense.

  • Listen fully and reflect back what you heard.
  • Find the part that is valid.
  • “That makes sense, given…”

Interpersonal effectiveness

Mindfulness of others

Pay attention to others with curiosity.

  • Observe what they say and do.
  • Drop assumptions and mind-reading.
  • Stay present instead of planning your reply.

Emotion regulation

Check the facts

Does my emotion fit the facts?

  • What happened? What am I assuming?
  • Is there a real threat? How likely is it?
  • Does the intensity fit the situation?

Emotion regulation

Opposite action

Act opposite to the urge when the emotion doesn't fit the facts.

  • Fear → approach. Anger → be gentle.
  • Sadness → get active. Shame → stay visible.
  • Do it all the way: words, face, posture.

Emotion regulation

Problem solving

When the emotion fits the facts, change the situation.

  • Describe the problem. Check the facts.
  • Brainstorm. Pick one solution.
  • Try it, then evaluate.

Emotion regulation

Accumulate positives

Build more positive experiences.

  • Short term: one pleasant thing every day.
  • Long term: steps toward your values.
  • Be mindful of good moments when they happen.

Emotion regulation

Build mastery

Do one thing each day that makes you feel capable.

  • Make it a little hard, but possible.
  • Increase the challenge slowly.
  • Notice the sense of accomplishment.

Emotion regulation

Cope ahead

Rehearse a hard situation before it happens.

  • Describe the situation and the emotion.
  • Pick the skills you'll use.
  • Imagine coping well, in detail.

Emotion regulation

PLEASE

Care for your body to lower emotional vulnerability.

  • treat PhysicaL illness · balanced Eating
  • avoid mood-Altering substances
  • balanced Sleep · get Exercise

Emotion regulation

Mindfulness of current emotion

Let the emotion be a wave.

  • Notice where you feel it in your body.
  • Don't push it away or hold on to it.
  • You are not your emotion.

Distress tolerance

STOP

Don't act on the urge yet.

  • Stop: freeze for a moment.
  • Take a step back. Breathe.
  • Observe, then Proceed mindfully.

Distress tolerance

Pros and cons

Weigh acting on the urge against resisting it.

  • Pros and cons of acting on the urge.
  • Pros and cons of resisting it.
  • Make the list before a crisis.

Distress tolerance

TIPP

Change your body chemistry fast.

  • Temperature: cold water on your face*
  • Intense exercise · Paced breathing
  • Paired muscle relaxation

Distress tolerance

Wise Mind ACCEPTS

Distract until the wave passes.

  • Activities · Contributing · Comparisons
  • Emotions (opposite) · Pushing away
  • Thoughts · Sensations

Distress tolerance

Self-soothe

Comfort yourself through your senses.

  • Vision · Hearing · Smell
  • Taste · Touch
  • Be gentle and kind to yourself.

Distress tolerance

IMPROVE the moment

Make a hard moment more bearable.

  • Imagery · Meaning · Prayer
  • Relaxing actions · One thing in the moment
  • brief Vacation · Encouragement

Distress tolerance

Radical acceptance

Accept reality as it is, completely.

  • Accept with mind, body and spirit.
  • Accepting is not approving.
  • Fighting reality turns pain into suffering.

Distress tolerance

Turning the mind

Choose acceptance again and again.

  • Notice when you are not accepting.
  • Turn your mind back toward acceptance.
  • Repeat as often as it takes.

Distress tolerance

Willingness

Do what the situation needs, wholeheartedly.

  • Notice willfulness: refusing, giving up.
  • Ask: what is needed right now?
  • Say yes to doing it.

Distress tolerance

Half-smiling and willing hands

Use your body to soften toward acceptance.

  • Relax your face. Lift your lips slightly.
  • Unclench your hands.
  • Rest them palms up.
